year_numbering: astronomical integers in JSON (1 BCE = 0); labels never show a year zero
theme: The world was doing other things
finale_thesis: Place the ten answers on one core and two of them land in the same year, 1977, for unrelated reasons: two spacecraft left for the outer solar system while the last natural case of smallpox was diagnosed. The Daily Trail shows simultaneity without claiming cause, and shows that our ten marks are a selection, not a sample of history.

target.definition: The year of discovery. The decree on the stone dates from 196 BC; the Greek text was first translated in 1803; Champollion announced decipherment in 1822. Sources disagree on the day in July.

free.text: By the end of that year, the French campaign in Egypt had already begun (28 June 1798).

context_free.text: The stone carries one decree in three scripts: Egyptian hieroglyphs, Demotic and Ancient Greek.

reveal.title: Found, made, read
reveal.text: Three dates, three different questions. The decree was made in 196 BC. The stone was found in July 1799. Its text was first read in translation in 1803, and the Egyptian scripts were transliterated in 1822.

reveal.title: Why the day is missing
reveal.text: Accounts give 15 July, 19 July and, in one encyclopedia, August 1799. We only say 1799.

uniqueness_proof.1976: 1976 is +1 calendar years from Last variola major case (1975); the clue needs +2.

cases.title: Sounds for the people
cases.lens: A moment outside the usual chronology
cases.question: In which year was the Hunminjeongeum, the document that introduced the Korean alphabet, published?

target.event: Publication of the Hunminjeongeum, about the ninth lunar month of 1446 (around October)
target.definition: The year of publication. The alphabet was devised earlier: it was introduced to the court in the 12th lunar month of 1443, which spans 30 December 1443 to 28 January 1444 in the Gregorian calendar, so the creation year is ambiguous and is not used.
target.calendar: Joseon lunisolar calendar, converted to Gregorian
target.discovery_vs_event: Publication, not invention. Invention falls across a Gregorian year boundary (1443 or 1444).

free.text: By the end of that year, the rain gauge had already been invented at Sejong's court (August 1441 by the lunar calendar).
By the end of that year, Yongbi eocheonga, the first book written in the new alphabet, had not yet been published (1447).
It was published four calendar years after the rain gauge was standardised (1442).

paid.text: By the end of that year, the Battle of Varna had already been fought (10 November 1444).

context_free.text: The name means 'The Correct Sounds for the Instruction of the People'.

reveal.title: Two ways to date a script
reveal.text: The alphabet was devised and shown to the court in the 12th lunar month of 1443. It was published in the ninth lunar month of 1446. The first is split across two Gregorian years; the second is not. The case asks for the publication.

reveal.title: Lunar months and Gregorian years
reveal.text: Joseon dated events by the lunar calendar. The same lunar month can fall in two Gregorian years, which is why 1443 or 1444 would both be defensible for the alphabet's creation.

uniqueness_proof.1441: 1441 is -1 calendar years from Rain gauge standardised (1442); the clue needs +4.
uniqueness_proof.1442: 1442 is +0 calendar years from Rain gauge standardised (1442); the clue needs +4.
uniqueness_proof.1443: 1443 is +1 calendar years from Rain gauge standardised (1442); the clue needs +4.
uniqueness_proof.1444: 1444 is +2 calendar years from Rain gauge standardised (1442); the clue needs +4.
uniqueness_proof.1445: 1445 is +3 calendar years from Rain gauge standardised (1442); the clue needs +4.

blockers: free f1 (Rain gauge invented) is V1
free f2 (Yongbi eocheonga published) is V1
free f3 (Rain gauge standardised) is V1
paid p1 (Battle of Varna) is V1

facts.claim: The base Hunminjeongeum was first published around October 1446 (Gregorian), in the 9th month of 1446 in the Korean calendar.
facts.note: UNESCO's nomination, seen in a search summary, says 9 October 1446. Wikipedia says the exact day is not known and that 9 October is an assumption. Year-level only.

facts.claim: The alphabet was introduced to the court in the 12th month of 1443 (30 December 1443 to 28 January 1444).
facts.note: Crosses a Gregorian year boundary. Not used as a boundary.

facts.claim: The rain gauge was invented in August 1441 (lunar) and standardised from 1442.
Yongbi eocheonga, the first work written in Hangul, was published in 1447.
The Battle of Varna was fought on 10 November 1444.

hold: Second opened source for the publication year (UNESCO nomination not opened). Clue ladder has one clue.
sample_player: The rain gauge was invented in 1441, so the publication was in 1441 or later. The first book in the alphabet was published in 1447, so the publication was by 1446: 1441 to 1446.
The third fragment says four calendar years after 1442, which is 1446.
Lock 1446.
editorial.miss_explanation: 1441 to 1446 fit the bounds. Only 1446 is four calendar years after the 1442 rain-gauge standard.

cases.title: The first count of a whole empire
cases.question: In which year was the first nationwide census of Han China taken?

target.event: The registration of households and persons recorded for the year 2 CE (Yuanshi 2)
target.definition: The year of the first nationwide census in Chinese history that left records. Exact totals are not used: sources disagree.
target.calendar: Han lunisolar era year Yuanshi 2, equal to 2 CE
target.discovery_vs_event: The count was recorded under era year Yuanshi 2.

free.text: By the end of that year, Emperor Ping had already taken the throne (17 October, 1 BCE).
By the end of that year, Emperor Ping had not yet died (3 February, 6 CE).
It was recorded in the second year of the Yuanshi era, an era that began in 1 CE.

paid.text: By the end of that year, the Yuanshi era name had already been proclaimed (1 CE).

context_free.text: There is no year 0 in BCE and CE dating: 1 BCE is followed directly by 1 CE.

reveal.title: A count with its disagreement showing
reveal.text: The 2 CE registration is the first nationwide census in Chinese history. Accounts give about 57.7 million people in one source and about 59.6 million in another. The chart shows both and says the figures are registrations, not a modern headcount.

reveal.title: BCE and CE
reveal.text: Year numbers jump from 1 BCE to 1 CE with no year 0, so the corridor 20 BCE to 20 CE has 40 years, not 41.

uniqueness_proof.0: 1 BCE is era year 0 (the era began in 1 CE); the clue needs era year 2.
uniqueness_proof.1: 1 CE is era year 1 (the era began in 1 CE); the clue needs era year 2.
uniqueness_proof.3: 3 CE is era year 3 (the era began in 1 CE); the clue needs era year 2.
uniqueness_proof.4: 4 CE is era year 4 (the era began in 1 CE); the clue needs era year 2.
uniqueness_proof.5: 5 CE is era year 5 (the era began in 1 CE); the clue needs era year 2.

blockers: free f1 (Emperor Ping takes the throne) is V1
free f2 (Emperor Ping dies) is V1
free f3 (Yuanshi era begins) is V1
paid p1 (Yuanshi era begins) is V1

facts.claim: The first nationwide census in Chinese history was taken in 2 AD.
facts.note: Seen in a search summary of historyofinformation.com and a reference to Bielenstein's 1947 study.

facts.claim: Wikipedia gives 57,671,400 people and 12,366,470 households. Other sources give about 59.6 million people and 12,233,062 households.
facts.note: Sources disagree. HOLD: needs the primary text (Book of Han ch. 28) via a source the editor can open. Shown as a range with a stated disagreement.

facts.claim: Emperor Ping reigned from 17 October 1 BC to 3 February 6 AD; era name Yuanshi 1 to 5 AD.

hold: Exact totals: HOLD (sources disagree, primary text not opened). Only the year is used.
Second opened source for the 2 CE census year.
sample_player: Emperor Ping took the throne in 1 BCE and died in 6 CE, so the census was between 1 BCE and 5 CE. That is six years: 1 BCE, then 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 CE. There is no year zero.
The third fragment says the second year of the Yuanshi era, which began in 1 CE. The first year is 1 CE, so the second is 2 CE.
Lock 2 CE.
editorial.miss_explanation: 1 BCE and 1 to 5 CE fit the bounds. Only 2 CE is the second year of an era whose first year was 1 CE.

cases.title: Greetings to the universe
cases.question: In which year were the two Voyager spacecraft launched?

target.event: Voyager 2 launches on 20 August 1977 and Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977
target.definition: The year both spacecraft launched. Voyager 2 launched first, on 20 August; Voyager 1 followed on 5 September.
target.discovery_vs_event: Event: launches. Not the Jupiter flybys (1979) and not leaving the heliosphere.

free.text: By the end of that year, the Viking 1 lander had already touched down on Mars (20 July 1976).
By the end of that year, Voyager 1 had not yet made its closest approach to Jupiter (5 March 1979).
They launched one calendar year after Concorde began scheduled passenger service (21 January 1976).

paid.text: By the end of that year, the last naturally occurring case of smallpox had already been diagnosed (October 1977).
By the end of that year, the 1978 laboratory smallpox outbreak in England had not yet happened.

context_free.text: Voyager 2 launched first, on 20 August; Voyager 1 followed on 5 September.

reveal.title: Two things happened in 1977
reveal.text: In 1977 two spacecraft left for the outer solar system, and the last natural case of smallpox was diagnosed in Somalia. Both are documented. Neither caused the other.

reveal.title: Your ten years on one core
reveal.text: The ten marks span two thousand years. Two of them, from different cases, fall in 1977. The gaps between neighbouring marks shrink from more than thirteen centuries to a few decades. The pack was selected by editors, so the pattern says as much about what is recorded as about the past.

uniqueness_proof.1976: 1976 is +0 calendar years from Concorde enters scheduled service (1976); the clue needs +1.
uniqueness_proof.1978: 1978 is +2 calendar years from Concorde enters scheduled service (1976); the clue needs +1.

blockers: free f1 (Viking 1 lands on Mars) is V1
free f2 (Voyager 1 at Jupiter) is V1
free f3 (Concorde enters scheduled service) is V1
paid p2 (Birmingham laboratory outbreak) is V1

facts.claim: Voyager 2 launched on 20 August 1977 and Voyager 1 on 5 September 1977.
facts.note: NASA's mission page opened and states launch 1977; the days come from Wikipedia.

facts.claim: Voyager 1's closest approach to Jupiter was on 5 March 1979.
Each spacecraft carries a record with greetings in 55 languages.
facts.note: NASA page seen in a search summary; page not opened. HOLD: not used anywhere in the pack.

facts.claim: The last known naturally occurring smallpox case was diagnosed in October 1977.

hold: The finale reuses 1977 from case 6; see AUDITS (cross-case leakage).
sample_player: The Viking 1 landing was in 1976, so the launches were in 1976 or later. Voyager 1's closest approach to Jupiter was in 1979, so the launches were by the end of 1978: 1976, 1977 or 1978.
The third fragment says one calendar year after Concorde began service in January 1976. One year after 1976 is 1977.
Lock 1977.
editorial.miss_explanation: 1976 to 1978 fit the bounds. Only 1977 is one calendar year after Concorde began scheduled service in January 1976.

connections.title: Same year, different day
connections.text: You have placed four marks: 1565, 1893, 1919, 1969. Look at the dates inside two of those cases. Sources disagree about the day of Concorde's first flight (1 or 2 March 1969) and of the Berlin Institute's opening (1 or 6 July 1919), but not about the year. A record can disagree about the day and still agree on the year.
connections.claim_type: editorial observation about source disagreement; the day-level disagreements are recorded in each case's facts

connections.title: How far apart are your marks?
connections.text: Placed in order, your seven marks are 1325, 1565, 1799, 1893, 1919, 1969, 1977. The gaps between neighbours are 240, 234, 94, 26, 50, 8 years. The pack was chosen by editors, so the gaps describe our selection as much as the past.
connections.claim_type: arithmetic on solved answers; the interpretation is labelled editorial
